# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

whys.g1: Eleanor's walk and my matinee are both trying a pair before buying, so they sit together under a plain name, and Ruth's answer is about what would make it worth more rather than a step she'd take, so it rightly stands on its own.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, and nothing is grouped that shouldn't be.

founder.order_why: The window question (screen 4) splits two context screens that carry the same heading, so the context step seems to restart after it rather than finishing first; the rest runs naturally from the problem, to the solution, to who asks and who gets a link.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both ask 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.' Screens 10 to 18 also pair each 'tell us' with a 'check what Keel wrote' and sometimes a 'what do you believe' for compatibility and adoption friction, which felt like the same point three times.
founder.missing: Nothing on money: no screen for the price ($599 glasses, $20/month Pro), what they spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, who pays (the wearer, HSA/FSA eligible), or the commitment step (order a pair with 15-day free returns). Without these I can't test the commercial side. Also small: screen 4 has a typo, 'aduts'.

PRIMARY.order_why: The phone-online question (screens 4-5) comes before I'm asked whether AirCaps would have helped at all, so I was answering about my phone before I knew why it mattered or whether I'd want the glasses.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 2 and 6 both send me back to my most recent conversation with hearing people, and screen 4 does it again with 'your last conversation', so it felt like the same moment asked three times in slightly different words.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what actually happened when I lost track: whether I asked people to repeat, lipread, used a captioning app or hearing aids, or just nodded along and dropped out. Nobody asked how noisy or fast the setting was either. I also expected a question on price and on whether the captions keep up with group talk, since those decide whether I'd wear the glasses.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what they have to do to start, Keel shows my steps back to check, which is where this belongs.
screens.why2: Wearing the glasses, pairing them to the phone and charging them daily are plain words to me and to my deaf and hard-of-hearing users.
screens.why3: These are steps my wearers take with their own hands every day, so they can answer from their own lives.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts: the setup and wear on first use, and the daily charging habit, which is the real ongoing catch; neither is nonsense or a duplicate.
screens.why5: The first row is my step word for word, and the belief tests exactly what I picked.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves, in the their-voice, and the belief can go either way, but the first row bundles two efforts (wearing and pairing), and its pairing half leans on Compatibility's phone-with-them-and-online ground; the charging row also reads like Keel's added habit step but shows no why.
screens.instead: Rows: Wear the glasses through every conversation · Charge the glasses every night (Keel's suggestion: the daily habit first use asks); belief: Most would wear the glasses through every conversation.

screens.why1: Once I've listed what people must do to start, picking the one step most likely to stop them is the obvious next move before the stranger test.
screens.why2: Wearing the glasses paired to the phone and charging them every day are words my wearers and I use all the time.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would put on paired glasses, or keep them charged, is something I hear about from our users every week.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts: my own setup row first, and Keel's charge-every-day suggestion last, which is the real new habit for 6-hour-a-day users.
screens.why5: My row is served word for word, and the belief and test read exactly as I typed it.
screens.why7: The measure, order and balance hold, and the bar can go either way, but my row bundles wearing with pairing to the phone, which edges onto Compatibility's phone-with-them test; the suggestion also shows no why beside it.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? · Wear the glasses through the day · Charge the glasses every day (suggested: power users wear them 6+ hours)

screens.why1: Just before the study goes out is the right place to decide whether to collect emails from people willing to try the glasses, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is everyday startup vocabulary to me, and the hint shows the exact line respondents will see and where the yeses land, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try AirCaps is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers the decision cleanly, both options are in plain words, and no escape is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: The respondent line 'Would you try this for real?' stays generic and leaks nothing, and my 'Yes' is kept as I picked it.

screens.why1: Choosing the interviewer belongs before launch, but for respondents who are deaf or hard of hearing, choosing a voice is the least important part of how they will meet the questions, so it feels abrupt here.
screens.why2: Daphne, Saskia, 'hear her' and '400 credits' are plain to me, though the hint is long and says 'voice' where my pick said 'face'.
screens.why3: I can play two five-second samples and pick one, which is something I can do myself.
screens.why4: The two voices are distinct, but for my people the true answer is often 'written questions first, voice secondary', or a captioned or signing interviewer, and that option is missing.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or my roles leaks into this choice, and it still means the preselected interviewer I locked.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get your questions? Written on screen with captions (voice optional): Daphne / Saskia / text only, no voice.

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it makes sense to pick how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Plain words: Daphne, read and tap, speak or type, let them choose; nothing I would need to read twice.
screens.why3: I know my people well; many will not want a spoken interviewer, and text-first is what I picked for them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete as formats, but for a Deaf audience a voice-led interviewer is an odd default and there is no note on ASL or captioned video for signers like the instructor who reads English as a second language.
screens.why5: It keeps my segment's wording, 'deaf and hard-of-hearing adults', and leaks nothing of the glasses to respondents.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or tap every answer) / AI interviewer Daphne, captioned on screen, answer by typing or talking / Let them choose when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer, the obvious next step is who gets the link, so it is the right last screen of sending.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the second option switches from 'I' to 'you' mid-line and points at a 'Contacts page' I have not seen anywhere in this flow, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know who I would reach first: people I know by name from years of TranscribeGlass users, and the HLAA chapters and online hard-of-hearing groups where one open link would land.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel search list, one open link for a group) are distinct and cover how I would reach this segment; a free-form escape is not needed for a routing choice.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps' product or roles is changed or leaked; the screen only asks how the links go out, and my pick of people by name is offered as written.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / People from a Keel search (pick a list; Keel makes a link for each, I send them) / A group, one open link (I post it where they already are; each person signs in with Google).

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title with the tally 3 of 3 holding, each card shows its deciding count against the bar (7 of 7 vs 5 of 7), and the page says the verdict is the worst card, so I know both the answer and why.
screens.why_b2: The count, the n of 7 and the bar of 5 are plain on every card, but Compatibility's "7 of 7 said yes or yes, with some steps" reads like a typo until I work out that it means two answer options pooled.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are the ones I checked, but the solution statement under the verdict is garbled ("wearing the glasses the app on the lightweight glasses shows... and gets back live captions"), so my own idea comes back recognisable but mangled.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what three holding beliefs mean for AirCaps or what I should do next; "What it measures" only explains how the verdict is computed.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible throughout, but a clean 7 of 7 sweep on all three beliefs is shown as "Holding up" with no note that seven people is a small group, or how many were screened out, and that lets a unanimous result from a few people read stronger than it is.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said yes or yes with some steps against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Three bars (Yes 4, With some steps 3, No 0) over 7 people with the marker at 5 read at once, and a fact rightly gets no 'only with help' row.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are exactly what I checked: for most deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, their phone was with them and online.
screens.why_b4: It tells me the phone-and-internet dependency is not my problem and points me to Adoption friction, and the three notes (borrow a pair for a matinee, a demo on a noisy walk) hint at a try-before-you-buy step.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and flagged as 'a lean, not a call', but the So line then states flatly that this 'is not what will stop them' and names Adoption friction as the blocker, which is firmer than seven yeses can carry, and the clipped question ('Had your phone with you and online?', 'last conversation' rather than my group conversation) is easy to skim past.
screens.instead: Ask 'On your last group conversation, did you have your phone with you and online?' and say: 'All 7 had it, 3 with some steps; a lean, not a call. The phone link looks unlikely to block you, so check Adoption friction next.'

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said it would have gone better, 7 of them a lot · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The strip makes the bar at 5 of 7 and the 7 for cells plain, but 'Better · 7 7 a lot · 0 a little' takes a second look to parse, and no-difference and worse are not drawn at zero, so I can't see the against side was empty.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Relative advantage and the belief line is word for word the one I checked, 'following more without asking anyone to repeat'.
screens.why_b4: 'All 7 imagined it going better' restates the count, and the pointer to Adoption friction is useful, but it never says what a unanimous 'a lot better' means for AirCaps, such as leading with that benefit.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 visible, calls it 'a lean, not a call', and flags the answer as a hypothetical asked with AirCaps in mind, so a 7-of-7 result is not oversold.
screens.instead: Draw no difference and worse at 0 beside better, and have the So line say: all 7 imagined their last conversation a lot better, a lean that following without asking anyone to repeat is worth leading with, though it is imagined, so whether they would actually wear the glasses is the real test, under Adoption friction.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, the 3 conditional yeses are split out, and the marker sits plainly at 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the glasses, paired to the phone' are the words I checked, though the asked line quietly drops the phone pairing and says 'whenever you talk with people'.
screens.why_b4: The So line defers to 'below', but all three gave the same catch (not looking odd), and the screen never says what that means for me, such as making discreet frames part of the pitch; the one quote below is about seating, not the glasses.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 stays visible, the conditional 3 are split out, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a unanimous 7 from reading as proof.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is; the other 3 only if they don't look odd in conversation, so how the frames look is the catch to answer before launch.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on 'Holding up' with '7 of 7 … bar 5 of 7' beside it, and the lead line 'Compatibility held, 7 of 7' ties the verdict to the number.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Adoption friction carry the exact belief lines I checked: phone with them and online, and wear the glasses paired to the phone.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what to do next, even though three people asking to borrow or demo a pair before ordering points straight at a trial or loaner offer beyond my 15-day returns, and the screen never says so.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible, but the Compatibility quotes under 'what steps did it take?' are about trialling the glasses and hall pickup, not about the phone being with them and online, so they look like support for a belief they never address; 'never saw it (Harriet, Ruth)' sits beside those two people's quotes one box up, and 3 on a condition shows only 1 quote, which is confusing.
screens.why_b6: I learn things I did not type: people want to try a pair at a matinee or on a noisy walk before buying, whether the lens is readable under stage lights matters, big-hall audience questions matter, and a one-side-deaf user gets by with an end seat and worries the glasses look odd.
screens.instead: Under Compatibility say 'nobody named a phone or connection problem', then say plainly: 3 of 7 want to try a pair first (matinee, noisy walk), so offer a loaner or demo; also test lens readability under stage lights, pickup of audience questions in a big hall, and whether the glasses look odd to the one-side-deaf who already get by with an end seat.

screens.why1: As the first screen it is obvious why it is asked: it checks I am someone who actually deals with hearing people regularly before asking about those conversations.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how deaf and hard-of-hearing people talk about everyone else, so it reads plainly to me on first go.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I talk with hearing people in a given week, at the shop, at work, with family.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and there is rightly no escape on a screener.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's "face to face" has dropped out, so a week of only texting or captioned calls with hearing people would still pass me through.
screens.why6: Short, one question, two options anyone can hold; "I'll read 2 options" is a touch stiff for a yes-or-no, but it says fine.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with a hearing person? Yes / No

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I lost the thread of one of those conversations this past week.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation with hearing people" is how I'd say it myself, and I'd answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost the thread at work, at the shop or at dinner this week; it happens to me, not to someone else.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it: some weeks I follow everything, and some weeks I'm lost at a noisy table, and the chips belong to the story box after a Yes.
screens.why5: It asks about my struggle in my own words ("hearing people" is what we say), with no hint of any product or anyone's plan.
screens.why6: One short question with "Yes or no" after it is easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the costly moment of losing track, not about talking with hearing people, which everyone here does, so both Yes and No are true of someone and the founder's band can be supported or refuted; it has the two fixed answers in order and no escape.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I lost track of a conversation with hearing people, showing me a captioning idea is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are words I use every day, so I get it on one read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what it's like to choose between watching someone's face and reading a screen, so I can judge this from my own life.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It's an idea card shown on purpose, and nothing in it uses odd insider terms for me or the people I talk with.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the second part repeats 'lightweight glasses' and 'the people nearby' from the first line, so it drags before the belief.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions of nearby speech. You wear the glasses, and the words people say appear inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Asking whether my phone was with me makes sense right after the glasses idea, but it jumps to my phone without saying why the glasses would need it, and *your last conversation* drops *with hearing people*, which the earlier screens were about.
screens.why2: *Had your phone with you and online?* is not a whole question, since it has no *Was it* or *Could you have*, and it asks two things at once: was my phone with me, and was it online.
screens.why3: I always know whether I had my phone on me and whether it had signal, so I can answer from my own day.
screens.why4: *Yes* and *No* fit, but *Yes, with some steps* is odd for whether I had my phone, and it gives no true answer when the phone was with me but had no signal.
screens.why5: Nothing of the company's plan leaks to me, but *your last conversation* has lost *with hearing people* and the occasion has drifted to any conversation at all.
screens.why6: The three options and *you can't tell* say well, but the stem is a clipped fragment that sounds wrong heard once, and I'd have to work out what is being asked.
screens.why7: This condition joins two facts (with me, and online), and it is true for nearly every deaf adult I know because our phones are our lifeline, so everyone answers Yes and nothing can count against; meanwhile what the pitch rests on, wearing glasses and reading captions while looking at the person, is not tested.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Could you have read captions on glasses while still watching the person's face? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: I just said I had my phone but with some steps, so asking what those steps were is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It hands back my own answer, 'yes, with some steps', and asks in everyday words what I had to do to get my phone online, which I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know what I did to get my phone out and connected, such as turning on data, finding wifi or charging it, because it is my own last conversation.
screens.why4: A box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: It stays on the phone being with me and online, which the idea card already set up, and it leaks no new product terms or roles.
screens.why6: It is short and is one question when spoken, with no list, symbols or parentheses, so I could hear it once and answer.

screens.why1: Right after the AirCaps card and the phone question, asking whether it would have helped me follow that conversation is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I'd understand it, but 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' is stiff; I'd say 'keep up with what people were saying' and it takes a second read to see that both halves are meant.
screens.why3: I know exactly how my last conversation with hearing people went and whether captions on glasses would have helped me keep up.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference or worse covers it, and I can't tell fits since I've never worn the glasses.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's description of AirCaps reaches me, and nothing of the founder's plan or labels for people like me leaks into the question or options.
screens.why6: One short question with four short options read as a list and one escape at the end, easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.why7: The measure, the four fixed options in order, the balance and the I can't tell escape all meet the card, but the occasion is any recent conversation rather than one that was too fast or noisy to follow, which bends the hard-case rule.
screens.instead: Think of the last time a conversation with hearing people got too fast or too noisy to follow. Would AirCaps have helped you keep up better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after I've pictured AirCaps on my last conversation, asking whether I'd actually wear the glasses to use it is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Wearing glasses when I talk with people is plain to me, and I'd answer it on first reading or with the captions on.
screens.why3: I know how I feel about wearing something on my face in a conversation, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: The four cover yes, a real catch for me (looking odd while I'm trying to fit in), probably not and no, with I can't tell apart, and none overlap.
screens.why5: It says 'talk with people' where my situation is talking with hearing people, so it stretches to conversations with deaf friends where I'd sign and never need captions; nothing of the founder's own plan leaks.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options as a list I can hold, and one escape said last.
screens.why7: Wearing the glasses whenever I talk is a new habit I take on myself, the options run yes, a conditional yes with my own catch, then probably not and no, so the belief could hold or fail, and I can't tell is there apart.
screens.instead: To use AirCaps, you'd wear the glasses whenever you talk with hearing people. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if they don't look odd in conversation · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: After I said whether I'd wear the glasses, asking what would make AirCaps worth it is reasonable, but it skips past my answer about wearing them and feels like a fresh, general question.
screens.why2: The words are plain to me, but it doesn't say back what I just answered about wearing the glasses, so I have to work out what it is following up on.
screens.why3: I know what would make captions in a conversation worth it to me, like keeping up in a noisy group or at the theatre, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card I was shown, and nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaks beyond that.
screens.why6: One short question that says easily and is heard once.
screens.instead: You said you'd wear the glasses only some of the time. What would make wearing them in a conversation worth it to you?
